rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet planned the pilgrimage for sacred Dhu'l-Qa'dah, when Arabian custom outlawed warfare, especially around Mecca, so he did not expect hostilities.
rows.anchor: the month of Dhu'l-Qa'dah, in which he intended to reach Mecca, was one of the four "sacred months" during which, in accordance with time-honoured Arabian custom, all warfare was outlawed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only 1,400–1,500 followers joined the pilgrimage, dressed as pilgrims and carrying only sheathed swords; Mecca sent cavalry and mobilized thousands to block them.
rows.anchor: of them dressed in the pilgrim's garb (ihram) and, apart from their sheathed swords, unarmed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After negotiations began, Muhammad sent Uthman as envoy; a false report of his murder led the followers to pledge steadfastness and fight to the death, later known as Bay'at ar-Ridwan.
rows.anchor: took, amid scenes of the greatest enthusiasm, a pledge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The treaty suspended warfare for ten years and deferred the pilgrimage to the following year, creating peaceful contact that opened Mecca to Islamic ideas.
rows.anchor: all warfare between Mecca and Medina should be suspended for ten years

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The treaty returned Meccan dependents who came to Muslims without guardians' consent but did not return Muslims who chose the Quraysh; Muhammad accepted this in keeping with the ban on religious coercion.
rows.anchor: the principle that "there shall be no coercion in matters of faith" (2:256)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hudaybiyyah's peaceful contacts impressed Meccans and brought growing numbers of converts; when Quraysh broke the truce two years later, Muhammad occupied Mecca almost without resistance, completing Islam's moral and political victory in Arabia.
rows.anchor: the Truce of Hudaybiyyah ushered in the moral and political victory of Islam over all Arabia

rows.speaker: all authorities
rows.claim: The authorities agree that the surah commemorating Hudaybiyyah's victory was revealed as the Prophet returned to Medina.
rows.anchor: In the consensus of all the authorities, the surah commemorating this victory was revealed during the Prophet's return march from Hudaybiyyah to Medina.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Freedom from faults belongs exclusively to God; every human being, however exalted, is bound to err on occasion.
rows.anchor: freedom from faults is an exclusive prerogative of God, and that every human being, however exalted, is bound to err on occasion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised completion is the fulfilment of Muhammad's mission, which the Hudaybiyyah truce clearly foreshadowed.
rows.anchor: to a fulfilment of thy mission", which the Truce of Hudaybiyyah clearly presaged

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gave the believers calm courage despite their small numbers and near lack of arms, enabling them to face the enemy's much greater force.
rows.anchor: endowed them, although they were few and practically unarmed, with calm courage in the face of the much more powerful forces of the enemy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reports the common view that this is a comparatively early Meccan surah, revealed shortly after surah 112.
rows.anchor: IT IS generally assumed that this is a

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some passages, especially 53:13–18, belong to a later period and allude to Muhammad's heavenly ascension about a year before the migration to Medina.
rows.anchor: However, some parts of it undoubtedly belong to a later period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah's title comes from the word an-najm at the beginning of its first verse.
rows.anchor: The title - explained in note 1 below - is taken from the word an-najm at the beginning of the first verse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad points readers to 12:40 as a parallel on the invented divine names and lack of warrant.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alleged mediation of goddesses and angels is wishful thinking; Asad says the same idea persists in saint veneration and the deification of people in higher religions.
rows.anchor: those goddesses, as well as the angels, would act as "mediators" between their worshippers and God: a wishful idea which lingers on even among adherents of higher religions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad rejects the weak, arbitrary view that two further gardens are for believers of lesser merit; their juxtaposition with the earlier pair instead suggests endless gardens, varied symbols of supreme bliss.
rows.anchor: As against this weak and somewhat arbitrary interpretation, it seems to me that the juxtaposition of "two other gardens" with. the "two" previously mentioned is meant to convey the idea of infinity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetorical challenge means: if people claim independence from any supreme power, why can they not restore the dying person's life? This connects the challenge with 56:57–74.
rows.anchor: If, then, as you claim, you are really independent of any Supreme Power, why do you not ...", etc., thus connecting with verses 57-74

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to his note on 6:73 for the phrase in this passage.
rows.anchor: See note 65 on the second paragraph of 6:73.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As-salam literally means “the Salvation”; Asad also refers readers to his note on 5:29.
rows.anchor: Lit., "the Salvation" (as-salam): see surah 5, note 29.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders muhaymin as the one who determines what is true and false, linking this usage to 5:48, where the term describes the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: For this rendering of muhaymin, see 5:48 - where this term is applied to the Qur'an - and the corresponding note 64.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because jabara combines restoring or setting right with compelling or subduing, Asad says al-jabbar is best rendered as the one who subdues wrong and restores right.
rows.anchor: the verb jabara - from which the noun jabbar is derived - combines the concepts of "setting right" or "restoring"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah's title, Al-Mumtahanah (“The Examined One”), comes from the command to examine women in verse 10.
rows.anchor: the injunction "examine them" in verse 10.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah was revealed months after Hudaybiyyah, no earlier than 7 AH and probably as late as early 8 AH.
rows.anchor: not earlier than the year 7 H. and probably as late as the beginning of 8 H.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah addresses believers' relations with unbelievers; although its first audience saw specific historical circumstances, its rules guide believers of every era.
rows.anchor: the import of the injunctions laid down in this surah cannot be restricted to that particular historical situation but has, as always in the Qur'an, a definite bearing on how believers of all times should behave

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Mecca-to-Medina context also points beyond its original setting to believers in every age facing persecution by people hostile to religious belief.
rows.anchor: In a more general sense, however, it is an allusion to the potential persecution of believers of all times by "those who are bent on denying the truth", i.e., those who are averse to religious beliefs as such.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads abadan in light of the noun abad's sense of an indefinite time or long duration, rendering it as “to last [until] …”.
rows.anchor: In view of the original connotation of the noun abad as "time" or "long time", i.e., of indefinite duration (Jawhari, Zamakhshari's Asas, Mughni, etc.), abadan is best rendered in the present context as "to last [until] ..."

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's filial love kept him from including his father in the declaration of enmity; after his father died an idolater, Abraham had to disavow him.
rows.anchor: his filial love prevented Abraham from including his father in his declaration of "enmity and hatred": although later - after his father had died as an idolater - Abraham could not but disavow him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Under the Hudaybiyyah treaty, Quraysh treated husbands as guardians and demanded return of Muslim women who had fled to Medina; Asad notes that the provision concerned persons under guardianship.
rows.anchor: The Quraysh took this stipulation to include also married women, whom they considered to be under the "guardianship" of their husbands. Accordingly, when several Meccan women embraced Islam against the will of their husbands and fled to Medina, the Quraysh demanded their forcible return to Mecca.

rows.speaker: Tabari
rows.claim: Al-Tabari reports that the Prophet required each emigrant woman to swear she left for love of God and His Apostle, not hatred of her husband, desire to move, or worldly advantage.
rows.anchor: swear before God that thou didst not leave for any reason save the love of God and His Apostle" (Tabari).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because only God knows a person's heart, a woman's affirmative oath was the only humanly attainable and legally sufficient proof of sincerity.
rows.anchor: a positive response of the woman concerned was to be regarded as the only humanly attainable - and, therefore, legally sufficient - proof of her sincerity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad generalizes the rule: absent contrary evidence, an adult's profession of faith obliges the community to accept that person as Muslim, whether man or woman.
rows.anchor: any adult person's declaration of faith, in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, makes it mandatory upon the community to accept that person - whether man or woman - as a Muslim

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When a woman embraces Islam and leaves her non-Muslim husband, the marriage is considered automatically annulled.
rows.anchor: marriage is considered, from the Islamic point of view, to have been automatically annulled

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A convert wife who leaves her non-Muslim husband is considered to break the contract and must refund her dower; if she cannot, the Muslim community must compensate him.
rows.anchor: the wife is to be considered the contract-breaking party and has, therefore, to refund the dower (mahr) which she received from him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If a Muslim wife abandons her husband, joins unbelievers, and renounces faith, the Muslim husband should treat the marriage as void; Asad points to verse 11.
rows.anchor: As for Muslim wives who, abandoning their husbands, go over to the unbelievers and renounce their faith, see verse 11.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Muslim community as a whole must indemnify a former non-Muslim husband when the wife cannot repay her dower, which explains the plural command “you shall return.”
rows.anchor: the Muslim community is obliged to indemnify the erstwhile husband: hence the plural form in the imperative "'you shall return" (lit., "give").

rows.speaker: Baghawi and Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Baghawi and Zamakhshari report six apostasy cases during Muhammad's lifetime, all before Mecca's conquest; by the Prophet's order, each Muslim husband received the original dower's equivalent from the communal treasury.
rows.anchor: there were only six such cases of apostasy in the lifetime of the Prophet (all of them before the conquest of Mecca in 8 H.); and in each case the Muslim husband was awarded by the communal treasury, on orders of the Prophet, the equivalent of the dower originally paid by him - (Baghawi and Zamakhshari).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad links the warning about befriending the condemned to 58:14 and its note 25.
rows.anchor: Cf. 58:14 and the corresponding note 25, which explains the reference to those "who would be friends with people whom God has condemned".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only people lacking real belief in the afterlife can remain neutral between right and wrong.
rows.anchor: only people without any real belief in a life to come can remain "neutral" between right and wrong

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deniers' hopelessness about seeing those in the graves reflects their rejection of resurrection.
rows.anchor: because they utterly reject the idea of resurrection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah argues that human earthbound knowledge cannot encompass the universe's mysteries, leaving people dependent on guidance through revelation.
rows.anchor: man's inability ever to encompass the mysteries of the universe

rows.speaker: Companions
rows.claim: The Companions also called the surah Al-Waqiyah (“The Preserving One”) or Al-Munjiyah (“The Saving One”).
rows.anchor: the Companions as "The Preserving One" (Al-Waqiyah) or "The Saving One" (Al-Munjiyah)

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains that these names describe the surah's power to save and preserve those who heed its lesson from suffering in the hereafter.
rows.anchor: the life to come (Zamakhshari).
